passages.title: A Rain Garden at School
passages.text:
A Rain Garden at School

After heavy rain, water sometimes rushes across hard surfaces such as paths, roofs and playgrounds. It may carry soil and litter into drains. A rain garden is a shallow planted area that helps collect some of this water. The water can soak slowly into the ground instead of flowing away at once.

At Green Lane School, the children noticed that a puddle often formed beside the playground path. Their teacher, Ms Rao, asked them to observe the area after rain. They marked where the water gathered and drew a simple map. The school gardener explained that a planted dip could help, but the adults first had to check the ground and choose a safe place.

The school made a small rain garden with permission and adult help. They loosened the soil and added plants suited to the local weather. The garden was not a pond: it was designed to drain after rain. The children learned that different plants need different amounts of water, so they did not water every plant in the same way.

After the next shower, the children watched from the path. Some water collected in the shallow garden, and the soil slowly absorbed it. A little water still ran towards the drain. The class recorded what they saw rather than claiming that the garden stopped all runoff.

Over several weeks, the children noticed new leaves and small insects among the plants. They also found a wrapper nearby and picked it up with their teacher. Ms Rao reminded them that a rain garden needs care: people must keep rubbish out, check the plants and make sure water can drain safely.

The class added their observations to a chart. They learned that watching a place before and after a change can help people ask better questions. The rain garden did not solve every water problem, but it gave the school a useful way to slow some rainwater, care for plants and learn from evidence.
